# Investigating Rate 6

Rate 6 is Eversource's proposed heat-pump rate. In winter (November–March) it charges
less for each kWh above 700 in a month than for the first 700. In April–October every kWh
pays the same rate.

This notebook does two things for Eversource's heat-pump homes (ResStock upgrade 02):

1. It compares annual energy bills under Rate 1, under Rate 6, and under a personalized
   version of Rate 6. In the personalized version, each home's winter discount starts at
   its own pre-heat-pump usage instead of at 700 kWh.
2. It measures how much of each home's extra electricity from switching to a heat pump
   (upgrade 02 minus upgrade 00) falls under 700 kWh and how much falls above it.

```{python}
#| label: params

_batch_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("../batch_config.yaml").read_text())

RATE6_SCENARIO = "default_ry1_r6_uncalibrated"
```

`MONTHS` only affects the 700 kWh share analysis at the end. The bill histograms use
the whole year.

## Annual energy bills after switching to a heat pump

Each bill comes from CAIRO's master bills table, which has one row per building per
month, plus an `Annual` row. `energy_total_bill` is the annual electricity, gas,
propane, and oil bill combined. Every histogram is weighted by ResStock's sample
weight, so the y-axis counts Eversource households, not ResStock buildings.

```{python}
#| label: load-annual-bills

def annual_bills(segment: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Annual energy bill and sample weight for every Eversource building in a segment."""
    return (
        load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, segment)
        .filter((pl.col("sb.electric_utility") == UTILITY) & (pl.col("month") == "Annual"))
        .select("bldg_id", "weight", "upgrade", BILL_COL)
        .collect()
    )


bills_rate1 = annual_bills(SEG_RATE1_HP)
bills_rate6 = annual_bills(SEG_RATE6_HP)
for label, bills in [("Rate 1", bills_rate1), ("Rate 6", bills_rate6)]:
    upgrades = bills["upgrade"].unique().to_list()
    assert upgrades == [2], f"{label}: expected upgrade 2 only, got {upgrades}"
    print(f"{label}: {bills.height:,} buildings, upgrade {upgrades[0]}")
bills_rate6.head(5)
```

All three histograms share the same x-axis, the 1st to 99th weighted percentile of all
three bill sets together, so they can be compared at a glance. The subtitle gives
each set's weighted median and mean.

```{python}
#| label: hist-helper

BIN_WIDTH = 250.0


def weighted_mean(df: pl.DataFrame, col: str) -> float:
    return float((df[col] * df["weight"]).sum() / df["weight"].sum())


def plot_annual_bill_hist(
    df: pl.DataFrame, title: str, x_limits: tuple[float, float]
) -> plt.ggplot:
    """Weighted histogram of annual energy bills on a fixed x-axis window."""
    binned = (
        df.with_columns(
            ((pl.col(BILL_COL) / BIN_WIDTH).floor() * BIN_WIDTH + BIN_WIDTH / 2).alias(
                "bin_center"
            )
        )
        .group_by("bin_center")
        .agg(pl.col("weight").sum().alias("households"))
    )
    lo, hi = x_limits
    breaks_fn = breaks_extended(n=8)
    median = weighted_quantile(df, BILL_COL, 0.5)
    mean = weighted_mean(df, BILL_COL)
    return (
        plt.ggplot(binned, plt.aes(x="bin_center", y="households"))
        + plt.geom_col(width=BIN_WIDTH * 0.9, fill=SB_COLORS["sky"])
        # coord_cartesian zooms without dropping bills outside the window.
        + plt.coord_cartesian(xlim=(lo, hi))
        + plt.scale_x_continuous(
            breaks=lambda _limits: breaks_fn((lo, hi)),
            labels=lambda xs: [f"${x:,.0f}" for x in xs],
        )
        + plt.scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda ys: [f"{y:,.0f}" for y in ys])
        + plt.labs(
            x="Annual energy bill",
            y="Households (weighted)",
            title=title,
            # Escaped: two bare "$" in one string turn on matplotlib mathtext.
            subtitle=f"Weighted median \\${median:,.0f}, mean \\${mean:,.0f}",
        )
        + theme_switchbox()
        + plt.theme(figure_size=(10.5, 4.5))
    )
```

### The personalized threshold

The third bill set is Rate 6 with one change. In the winter months, the block boundary is each home's
own upgrade-00 electricity use that month instead of 700 kWh:

- **April–October:** unchanged. Every kWh pays the single Block 1 rate.
- **November–March:** kWh up to the home's pre-heat-pump usage pay the Block 1 rate, and
  only the incremental kWh above it pay the cheaper Block 2 rate.
- If a home's winter usage stayed the same or went down (for example, it already heated
  with electric resistance), every kWh pays the Block 1 rate.

The filed distribution charges are `$0.09431` (Block 1) and `$0.07517` (Block 2) per kWh.
The tariff CAIRO bills with folds per-kWh riders into both blocks, so its rates are higher.
The riders are the same in both blocks, so they cancel and only the difference between
the blocks matters. We read the block rates, the 700 kWh threshold, and the winter months
directly from the Rate 6 tariff JSON this batch was run with.

```{python}
#| label: rate6-tariff

tariff_rate6 = load_tariff_json(STATE, UTILITY, f"{UTILITY}_rate6", RDP_REF)
_structure = tariff_rate6["energyratestructure"]
WINTER_PERIOD = next(i for i, tiers in enumerate(_structure) if len(tiers) > 1)
BLOCK1_RATE = float(_structure[WINTER_PERIOD][0]["rate"])
BLOCK2_RATE = float(_structure[WINTER_PERIOD][1]["rate"])
RATE6_THRESHOLD_KWH = float(_structure[WINTER_PERIOD][0]["max"])
WINTER_MONTHS = [
    MONTH_ORDER[i]
    for i, row in enumerate(tariff_rate6["energyweekdayschedule"])
    if row[0] == WINTER_PERIOD
]
print(f"Block 1: ${BLOCK1_RATE:.5f}/kWh   Block 2: ${BLOCK2_RATE:.5f}/kWh")
print(f"Block gap: ${BLOCK1_RATE - BLOCK2_RATE:.5f}/kWh (filed: $0.09431 - $0.07517 = $0.01914)")
print(f"Threshold: {RATE6_THRESHOLD_KWH:,.0f} kWh   Winter months: {WINTER_MONTHS}")
```

Rather than rebuild the whole bill, we start from each home's actual Rate 6 bill and
change only the winter energy charge. For one winter month, let $B$ be upgrade-00 kWh,
$A$ be upgrade-02 kWh, $r_1$ the Block 1 rate, and $r_2$ the Block 2 rate:

- Rate 6 charges $r_1 \min(A, 700) + r_2 \max(A - 700, 0)$
- the personalized rate charges $r_1 \min(A, B) + r_2 \max(A - B, 0)$

Their difference simplifies to

$$(r_2 - r_1)\,\big[\max(A - B, 0) - \max(A - 700, 0)\big]$$

We add that difference to the Rate 6 bill for each winter month. Fixed charges, supply,
gas, and fuel bills stay exactly as CAIRO computed them. kWh comes from `elec_grid_kwh`
in the upgrade-00 and upgrade-02 Rate 6 runs, the grid consumption CAIRO bills on.

```{python}
#| label: winter-kwh

def winter_grid_kwh(segment: str, name: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Monthly grid kWh in the Rate 6 winter months for every Eversource building."""
    return (
        load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, segment)
        .filter(
            (pl.col("sb.electric_utility") == UTILITY) & pl.col("month").is_in(WINTER_MONTHS)
        )
        .select("bldg_id", "month", pl.col("elec_grid_kwh").alias(name))
        .collect()
    )


winter_kwh = winter_grid_kwh(SEG_RATE6_BASE, "kwh_before").join(
    winter_grid_kwh(SEG_RATE6_HP, "kwh_after"), on=["bldg_id", "month"], how="inner"
)
assert winter_kwh.height == bills_rate6.height * len(WINTER_MONTHS)
winter_kwh.head(5)
```

```{python}
#| label: personalized-bills

personal_adjustment = (
    winter_kwh.with_columns(
        (
            (BLOCK2_RATE - BLOCK1_RATE)
            * (
                (pl.col("kwh_after") - pl.col("kwh_before")).clip(lower_bound=0)
                - (pl.col("kwh_after") - RATE6_THRESHOLD_KWH).clip(lower_bound=0)
            )
        ).alias("adjustment")
    )
    .group_by("bldg_id")
    .agg(pl.col("adjustment").sum())
)
bills_personal = bills_rate6.join(personal_adjustment, on="bldg_id", how="left").with_columns(
    (pl.col(BILL_COL) + pl.col("adjustment")).alias(BILL_COL)
)
assert bills_personal["adjustment"].null_count() == 0
print(
    bills_personal.select(
        pl.col("adjustment").mean().alias("mean_change_vs_rate6"),
        pl.col("adjustment").min().alias("min_change_vs_rate6"),
        pl.col("adjustment").max().alias("max_change_vs_rate6"),
        (pl.col("adjustment") > 0).mean().alias("share_paying_more"),
    )
)
```

A positive adjustment means the home pays more than under Rate 6. That happens when its
pre-heat-pump winter usage was above 700 kWh: its own threshold is higher, so fewer kWh
get the discount. A negative adjustment means the home used less than 700 kWh before
switching, so more of its winter load gets the Block 2 rate.

## Who pays more under the personalized threshold

Each point is one Eversource building. The y-axis is its upgrade-02 annual energy bill
under the personalized threshold minus its Rate 6 bill: above the dotted line the home
pays more, below it the home pays less. Electricity on the x-axis is upgrade-00 grid
consumption, `elec_grid_kwh` from before the heat pump. Winter is November through March.
Color is the home's heating type before the heat pump, from
`postprocess_group.heating_type_v2`.

```{python}
#| label: bill-change-scatter-data

annual_kwh = (
    load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_RATE6_BASE)
    .filter((pl.col("sb.electric_utility") == UTILITY) & (pl.col("month") == "Annual"))
    .select(
        "bldg_id",
        "upgrade",
        pl.col("elec_grid_kwh").alias("annual_kwh"),
        "postprocess_group.heating_type_v2",
    )
    .collect()
)
assert annual_kwh["upgrade"].unique().to_list() == [0]
winter_kwh_total = winter_kwh.group_by("bldg_id").agg(pl.col("kwh_before").sum().alias("winter_kwh"))
# Paul Tol's bright palette. The brand colors sit too close together to separate
# five heating types on one scatter.
HEATING_COLORS = {
    "Natural gas": "#4477AA",
    "Oil/propane": "#EE6677",
    "Electric resistance": "#228833",
    "Existing heat pump": "#AA3377",
    "Other": "#66CCEE",
}
bill_change_scatter = add_heating_label(
    bills_personal.select(
        "bldg_id",
        "weight",
        pl.col("adjustment").alias("bill_change"),
        # The adjustment is already the winter-only difference.
        pl.col("adjustment").alias("winter_bill_change"),
    )
    .join(annual_kwh, on="bldg_id", how="inner")
    .join(winter_kwh_total, on="bldg_id", how="inner"),
    code_col="postprocess_group.heating_type_v2",
)
# Largest heating type first, so the smaller groups are drawn on top.
_draw_order = (
    bill_change_scatter["heating_label"]
    .value_counts()
    .sort("count", descending=True)["heating_label"]
    .to_list()
)
bill_change_scatter = bill_change_scatter.with_columns(
    pl.col("heating_label")
    .replace_strict({label: i for i, label in enumerate(_draw_order)})
    .alias("_draw"),
    pl.col("heating_label").cast(pl.Enum(HEATING_ORDER)),
).sort("_draw")
assert bill_change_scatter.height == bills_rate6.height
print(bill_change_scatter["heating_label"].value_counts(sort=False))
bill_change_scatter.head(5)
```

```{python}
#| label: heating-scatter-helper

def plot_heating_scatter(df, x, y, x_label, y_label, title):
    """Heating-type scatter of a bill change against electricity use."""
    return (
        plt.ggplot(df, plt.aes(x=x, y=y, color="heating_label"))
        + plt.geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dotted", color="gray")
        + plt.geom_point(alpha=0.75, size=1.5)
        + plt.scale_color_manual(values=HEATING_COLORS, name="Heating type")
        + plt.scale_x_log10(labels=lambda values: [f"{value:,.0f}" for value in values])
        + plt.scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda values: [f"${value:,.0f}" for value in values])
        + plt.labs(x=x_label, y=y_label, title=title)
        + theme_switchbox()
        + plt.theme(figure_size=(10.5, 4.5))
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-change-vs-annual-kwh
#| fig-cap: "Change in the upgrade-02 annual energy bill from moving Rate 6's 700 kWh winter threshold to each home's own pre-heat-pump usage, against upgrade-00 annual electricity use."

plot_heating_scatter(
    bill_change_scatter,
    "annual_kwh",
    "bill_change",
    "Annual electricity use before the heat pump (kWh, log scale)",
    "Bill change, personalized minus Rate 6",
    "Personalized threshold vs Rate 6, by pre-heat-pump annual use",
)
```

On the winter chart, the straight line that lifts off zero near 3,500 kWh is homes whose
electricity use went up. Past that point their pre-heat-pump winter use is above 700 kWh
a month, so Rate 6 discounts some of that pre-retrofit load and the personalized rate
does not. The gap grows by about 1.9 cents for each of those kWh. Electric-resistance and
existing heat-pump homes sit above the line: their use fell or stayed flat, so they lose
the Rate 6 discount without gaining a personalized one.

### Who pays more, and who pays less

A positive bill change means the home pays more under the personalized threshold than
under Rate 6. A negative change means it pays less. The pies below are the heating-type
mix of each group, weighted by ResStock's sample weight. Homes whose bill does not
change are left out of both charts.

```{python}
#| label: heating-composition

def heating_composition(pays_more: bool) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Weighted heating-type shares for homes whose bill goes up, or down."""
    subset = bill_change_scatter.filter(
        pl.col("bill_change") > 0 if pays_more else pl.col("bill_change") < 0
    )
    total_weight = float(subset["weight"].sum())
    counted = (
        subset.with_columns(pl.col("heating_label").cast(pl.String))
        .group_by("heating_label")
        .agg(pl.col("weight").sum().alias("weight"), pl.len().alias("n"))
    )
    composition = (
        pl.DataFrame({"heating_label": HEATING_ORDER})
        .join(counted, on="heating_label", how="left")
        .with_columns(pl.col("weight").fill_null(0.0), pl.col("n").fill_null(0))
        .with_columns((pl.col("weight") / total_weight * 100).alias("pct"))
    )
    labels = [f"{pct:.1f}%" if pct < 1 else f"{pct:.0f}%" for pct in composition["pct"].to_list()]
    return composition.with_columns(pl.Series("label", labels))


def plot_heating_pie(composition: pl.DataFrame, title: str):
    """Pie of heating-type shares. Plotnine 0.15 has no polar coordinates."""
    import matplotlib.pyplot as mpl

    theme_switchbox()  # registers GT Planar and IBM Plex Sans
    fig, ax = mpl.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 4.5))
    fig.patch.set_facecolor("white")
    wedges, _ = ax.pie(
        composition["pct"].to_list(),
        colors=[HEATING_COLORS[name] for name in composition["heating_label"].to_list()],
        startangle=90,
        counterclock=False,
        wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white", "linewidth": 1.5},
    )
    ax.legend(
        wedges,
        [
            f"{name}   {label}"
            for name, label in zip(composition["heating_label"], composition["label"], strict=True)
        ],
        title="Heating type",
        loc="center left",
        bbox_to_anchor=(0.95, 0.5),
        frameon=False,
        prop={"family": "IBM Plex Sans", "size": 11},
        title_fontproperties={"family": "GT Planar", "size": 13},
    )
    ax.set_title(
        title,
        loc="left",
        fontfamily="GT Planar",
        fontweight="bold",
        fontsize=15,
        color="black",
    )
    return fig


composition_pays_more = heating_composition(pays_more=True)
composition_pays_less = heating_composition(pays_more=False)
n_unchanged = bill_change_scatter.filter(pl.col("bill_change") == 0).height
print(f"{n_unchanged:,} buildings have no bill change and are left out")
print(composition_pays_more.select("heating_label", "n", "pct"))
print(composition_pays_less.select("heating_label", "n", "pct"))
```

```{python}

#| fig-cap: "Heating-type mix of Eversource homes whose upgrade-02 bill is higher under the personalized threshold than under Rate 6. Shares are weighted."

display_figure(
    plot_heating_pie(
        composition_pays_more,
        "Homes that pay more under the personalized rate",
    )
)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Heating-type mix of Eversource homes whose upgrade-02 bill is lower under the personalized threshold than under Rate 6. Shares are weighted."

display_figure(

    )
)
```

### Bill change from Rate 6 to the personalized rate

These are the same four bins used in the other heat-pump reports. Green is a lower bill
under the personalized rate than under Rate 6. Red is a higher bill. A change of exactly
$0 is counted in the $0–$1,000 loss bin, which is how that chart is defined. Nobody's
bill moves by $1,000 or more, so the dark-green and dark-red bins are empty. For
electric-resistance and existing heat-pump homes, much of the red bar is a bill that
does not change at all: about 30% and 13% of those homes, weighted.

```{python}
#| label: fig-quadrant-by-heating
#| fig-cap: "Weighted share of homes, by heating type, whose annual bill rises or falls when the Rate 6 winter threshold is replaced with each home's pre-heat-pump usage."

rows = [
    (
        label,
        bill_change_scatter.filter(pl.col("heating_label") == label).select(
            pl.col("bill_change").alias("delta"),
            "weight",
        ),
    )
    for label in HEATING_ORDER
]
plot_bill_change_quadrant_comparison(
    rows,
    title="Bill change from Rate 6 to the personalized rate, by heating type",
)
```

## Share of incremental load under and above 700 kWh

Change `MONTHS` in the params cell to choose the months. `[1]` is January. A longer list,
such as `[11, 12, 1, 2, 3]`, averages each building's monthly shares across those months.
A month with no change in electricity use is left out of that average. The load is
ResStock's monthly `out.electricity.total.energy_consumption`, in kWh. It is the simulated
electricity use, not the scaled kWh CAIRO bills.

### Which buildings

Utility assignment lives in its own file. ResStock metadata has no utility column.

```{python}
#| label: eversource-buildings

utility_assignment = pl.read_parquet(
    RESSTOCK_ROOT / "metadata_utility" / f"state={STATE}" / "utility_assignment.parquet"
)
eversource_ids = (
    utility_assignment.filter(pl.col("sb.electric_utility") == UTILITY)
    .get_column("bldg_id")
    .to_list()
)
print(f"{len(eversource_ids):,} buildings with sb.electric_utility = {UTILITY}")
utility_assignment.filter(pl.col("sb.electric_utility") == UTILITY).head(5)
```

### Monthly electricity, before and after

Each upgrade directory holds one monthly parquet per building, named
`{bldg_id}-{upgrade}.parquet`, with one row per month.

```{python}
#| label: load-monthly

def monthly_kwh(upgrade: str, bldg_ids: list[int], months: list[int]) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Monthly total electricity kWh for the requested buildings and months."""
    upgrade_int = int(upgrade)
    directory = RESSTOCK_ROOT / "load_curve_monthly" / f"state={STATE}" / f"upgrade={upgrade}"
    paths = [str(directory / f"{bldg_id}-{upgrade_int}.parquet") for bldg_id in bldg_ids]
    missing = [path for path in paths if not Path(path).exists()]
    if missing:
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"{len(missing):,} monthly files missing under {directory}, e.g. {missing[0]}"
        )
    return (
        pl.scan_parquet(paths)
        .filter(pl.col("month").is_in(months))
        .select("bldg_id", "month", pl.col(KWH_COL).alias("kwh"))
        .collect()
    )


kwh_before = monthly_kwh(UPGRADE_BEFORE, eversource_ids, MONTHS)
kwh_after = monthly_kwh(UPGRADE_AFTER, eversource_ids, MONTHS)
print(f"Upgrade {UPGRADE_BEFORE}: {kwh_before.height:,} building-months")
print(f"Upgrade {UPGRADE_AFTER}: {kwh_after.height:,} building-months")
kwh_before.head(5)
```

### Split the incremental kWh at 700

For one building-month, let $B$ be upgrade-00 kWh and $A$ be upgrade-02 kWh.
The incremental load is $A - B$. Of that increment:

- the part under the threshold is $\min(A, 700) - \min(B, 700)$
- the part above the threshold is $\max(A - 700, 0) - \max(B - 700, 0)$

Those two parts add up to $A - B$. Each share is that part divided by $A - B$.
When several months are requested, the building's result is the average of its
monthly shares. Months with $A = B$ have no incremental load, so they are dropped
from the average.

```{python}
#| label: block-shares

def incremental_block_shares(
    before: pl.DataFrame,
    after: pl.DataFrame,
    threshold_kwh: float,
) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Share of incremental kWh under and above `threshold_kwh`, averaged over months."""
    monthly = (
        before.rename({"kwh": "kwh_before"})
        .join(after.rename({"kwh": "kwh_after"}), on=["bldg_id", "month"], how="inner")
        .with_columns(
            (pl.col("kwh_after") - pl.col("kwh_before")).alias("incremental_kwh"),
            (
                pl.min_horizontal(pl.col("kwh_after"), threshold_kwh)
                - pl.min_horizontal(pl.col("kwh_before"), threshold_kwh)
            ).alias("incremental_kwh_under"),
            (
                (pl.col("kwh_after") - threshold_kwh).clip(lower_bound=0)
                - (pl.col("kwh_before") - threshold_kwh).clip(lower_bound=0)
            ).alias("incremental_kwh_above"),
        )
        .with_columns(
            pl.when(pl.col("incremental_kwh") != 0)
            .then(pl.col("incremental_kwh_under") / pl.col("incremental_kwh"))
            .otherwise(None)
            .alias("share_under"),
            pl.when(pl.col("incremental_kwh") != 0)
            .then(pl.col("incremental_kwh_above") / pl.col("incremental_kwh"))
            .otherwise(None)
            .alias("share_above"),
        )
    )
    return monthly.group_by("bldg_id").agg(
        pl.col("share_under").mean().alias("share_under"),
        pl.col("share_above").mean().alias("share_above"),
        pl.col("incremental_kwh").sum().alias("incremental_kwh"),
        pl.col("incremental_kwh_under").sum().alias("incremental_kwh_under"),
        pl.col("incremental_kwh_above").sum().alias("incremental_kwh_above"),
        pl.col("share_under").is_not_null().sum().alias("n_months"),
    )


shares = incremental_block_shares(kwh_before, kwh_after, THRESHOLD_KWH).sort("bldg_id")
n_missing = shares.filter(pl.col("share_under").is_null()).height
print(
    f"{shares.height:,} buildings. {n_missing:,} have no electricity change "
    f"in months {MONTHS}, so their shares are null."
)
shares.head(8)
```

`share_under` and `share_above` are the result: fractions of incremental load, averaging
to the requested months. The kWh columns are the sums across those months, so you can
see the loads behind the average.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shares

month_label = ", ".join(str(month) for month in MONTHS)
_shares_gt = (
    GT(shares.head(20), rowname_col="bldg_id")
    .fmt_percent(columns=["share_under", "share_above"], decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(
        columns=["incremental_kwh", "incremental_kwh_under", "incremental_kwh_above"],
        decimals=0,
    )
    .cols_label(
        share_under="Under 700 kWh",
        share_above="Above 700 kWh",
        incremental_kwh="Incremental kWh",
        incremental_kwh_under="kWh under",
        incremental_kwh_above="kWh above",
        n_months="Months used",
    )
    .tab_header(title=f"First 20 Eversource buildings, months {month_label}")
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_shares_gt)
```

A quick check that the two shares add to 1 wherever the building's electricity changed.

```{python}
#| label: sanity-check

defined = shares.filter(pl.col("share_under").is_not_null())
share_gap = (defined["share_under"] + defined["share_above"] - 1).abs().max()
kwh_gap = (
    defined["incremental_kwh_under"] + defined["incremental_kwh_above"] - defined["incremental_kwh"]
).abs().max()
print(f"Largest |share_under + share_above - 1|: {share_gap:.2e}")
print(f"Largest |kWh under + kWh above - incremental kWh|: {kwh_gap:.2e}")
print(
    defined.select(
        pl.col("share_under").mean().alias("mean_share_under"),
        pl.col("share_above").mean().alias("mean_share_above"),
        pl.col("share_under").median().alias("median_share_under"),
    )
)
```
